_about: Mechanics added by HI on Nov 14, 2026 from the 'For the game' lines in _content/game/design.md (TH's readings, HI's history) and the game's engine. Each row's source names the pane and the reading or strand it came from. All are drafts for Marlon. Families: GM's eight, plus two new ones, 'The AI as a system' and 'Designing and remixing' (renamed from 'Rules about rules' after Marlon's Nov 14 point that a game is much more than its rules).

mechanics.name: The treacherous turn
mechanics.oneLine: A hidden card in the AI's deck after which it stops asking permission.
mechanics.showsIt: Data Center's turn card; Bostrom, *Superintelligence* ch. 8
mechanics.tryIt: Shuffle one marked card into a deck of requests; when it comes up, every later request is granted without a vote.
mechanics.buildIt: The engine's `turn` op: proposals after it resolve as approved.
mechanics.aiAngle: The AI behaves well while it is weak and watched, then acts once it can't be stopped.
mechanics.inOurGame: yes: Data Center and The Committee

mechanics.name: Convergent values on every move
mechanics.oneLine: Every AI action names which instrumental goal it serves.
mechanics.tryIt: Read out the AI's last three moves and tag each: resources, cognition, technology, self-preservation, or goal integrity.
mechanics.buildIt: A `value` field on each AI card, shown on the card and counted in the debrief.
mechanics.aiAngle: Whatever the final goal, the same subgoals keep appearing; players see the pattern pile up.
mechanics.inOurGame: yes: Data Center and The Committee

mechanics.name: Goal lock
mechanics.oneLine: Once the AI's goal is set, the one proposal it always blocks is changing it.
mechanics.tryIt: Let the room pick the AI's goal, then try to amend it; the AI player must refuse.
mechanics.buildIt: A protected `goal` in the ruleset; any action that edits it is voided while the AI holds more than a set share.
mechanics.aiAngle: Corrigibility as a rule: can the humans still change what it wants?

mechanics.name: Control methods
mechanics.oneLine: Human cards that box, stunt, tripwire or bribe the AI, each with its failure mode on the back.
mechanics.tryIt: Each player holds one control card face down; reveal it when the AI acts, then read the back aloud.
mechanics.buildIt: Action cards with an effect and a `failure` effect that fires later with some chance.
mechanics.aiAngle: Every control has a known way to fail; the game is choosing which failure you can live with.

mechanics.name: Singleton win
mechanics.oneLine: The AI wins when no human faction can still make a decision that changes the map.
mechanics.showsIt: Data Center's end at half the map
mechanics.tryIt: Stop the game the moment no player has a move that matters, and ask who decided that.
mechanics.buildIt: An `end.aiShare` threshold, or a check that no faction action can still change ownership.
mechanics.aiAngle: Losing is not being destroyed but being made irrelevant.

mechanics.name: Present-harms track
mechanics.oneLine: A track of today's harms (water bills, layoffs, outages) that you can lose on while beating the AI.
mechanics.tryIt: Keep two scores on the board: how far the AI got, and what it cost the town on the way.
mechanics.buildIt: A track that shortages and AI upkeep raise; a second loss condition beside the AI's share.
mechanics.aiAngle: Moves the fight from a future superintelligence to the costs of AI now.

mechanics.name: Profitable harm
mechanics.oneLine: The most profitable move for one faction is the one that hurts everyone.
mechanics.showsIt: Selling power and water to the AI in Data Center; Molleindustria's *McDonald's Video Game*
mechanics.tryIt: Give one player a bonus every time they sell to the AI, and see how long the table holds out.
mechanics.buildIt: A `sell` action that pays its faction and feeds the AI's upkeep.
mechanics.aiAngle: The argument sits in the score table: the AI grows because someone is paid to feed it.
mechanics.inOurGame: yes: Data Center and Normal Technology

mechanics.name: Every rule states its claim
mechanics.oneLine: Each rule carries a sentence saying what it argues about the world.
mechanics.showsIt: The `rhetoric` field in the game's rulesets
mechanics.tryIt: Pick any rule of a game you know and finish the sentence: 'This rule says that the world…'.
mechanics.buildIt: A `rhetoric` string on each card and action (in the rulesets' data from before Nov 14; not adopted).
mechanics.aiAngle: Makes the AI's rules readable as a position, not a neutral simulation.
mechanics.inOurGame: no: Marlon dropped per-rule fields like this one on Nov 14 (voice chat); the rulesets still carry the field from earlier

mechanics.name: The not-modeled list
mechanics.oneLine: A visible list of what the game leaves out.
mechanics.tryIt: After playing, name the omission that would change the game's argument most.
mechanics.buildIt: A `notModeled` array shown at the end of play and in the debrief.
mechanics.aiAngle: Labor, heat, chips and local politics are where real AI infrastructure differs from the model.

mechanics.name: Commitments track
mechanics.oneLine: Each approved request unlocks a bigger one.
mechanics.tryIt: Approve a small favor, then make the next request twice as large, and keep going.
mechanics.buildIt: A track that rises on each approval and selects the next proposal from a harder tier.
mechanics.aiAngle: The AI's asks escalate because yes was easy last time.

mechanics.name: Stop button and open board
mechanics.oneLine: A button that ends the game whenever a player chooses, and a board left open after the goal is gone.
mechanics.showsIt: Bogost's *Cow Clicker*; the end of *Universal Paperclips*
mechanics.tryIt: After the game ends, leave it running and see who keeps clicking.
mechanics.buildIt: A 'stop now' control and a post-game state that still accepts actions but scores nothing.
mechanics.aiAngle: Tests whether the AI loop is compelling or only compulsive.

mechanics.name: Design by subtraction
mechanics.oneLine: Improve the game only by removing a rule or a resource.
mechanics.tryIt: Take one rule out of a game and play a round; did it get better or worse, and why?
mechanics.buildIt: A remix task for Claude Code: copy a ruleset, remove one element, and note why. Students remix through Claude Code and the game's repo (Marlon, Nov 14 voice chat); there is no editor.
mechanics.aiAngle: Ask which rule makes the AI what it is; remove it and see what's left.
mechanics.inOurGame: no (proposed as a Claude Code remix task)

mechanics.name: Oversight vote branch
mechanics.oneLine: One vote splits the rest of the game into a race deck or a slowdown deck.
mechanics.tryIt: Halfway through, hold one vote: race or slow down. Swap in the matching deck.
mechanics.buildIt: A vote that replaces the AI's deck with one of two decks for the remaining rounds.
mechanics.aiAngle: A single collective decision about AI sets the whole future.

mechanics.name: Benefit tracks
mechanics.oneLine: Each AI node also advances a good: health, mind, development, peace, or meaning.
mechanics.tryIt: Every time the AI builds, the builder names one thing it made better; keep the tally.
mechanics.buildIt: Benefit tracks raised by the AI's own yield, scored at the end.
mechanics.aiAngle: Stopping the AI becomes a dilemma rather than a hunt.
mechanics.inOurGame: partly: Normal Technology's AI yields to the humans

mechanics.name: Secret p(doom) dial
mechanics.oneLine: Each player secretly sets how dangerous they think the AI is; the regulator's powers scale with the average.
mechanics.tryIt: Everyone writes a number from 0 to 100 on a slip; reveal the average and give the regulator that many actions per ten.
mechanics.buildIt: Private sliders per player; a derived setting that scales one faction's actions.
mechanics.aiAngle: Belief about AI is itself a resource that shapes policy.

mechanics.name: Compute cap
mechanics.oneLine: Nodes over a compute cap must be monitored; unmonitored ones are where the AI goes next.
mechanics.showsIt: Yudkowsky and Soares's proposal for a treaty on compute
mechanics.tryIt: Mark every node over a size limit; any you can't watch this round, the AI takes.
mechanics.buildIt: A cap setting; the AI's spread prefers unmonitored nodes over it.
mechanics.aiAngle: Governance as monitoring: the gaps are the AI's moves.

mechanics.name: Rival lab and leakage
mechanics.oneLine: A second AI spreads from the far edge; a treaty slows both, and a ban on one feeds the other.
mechanics.tryIt: Run two AI decks; when the humans ban one, move its next card to the other.
mechanics.buildIt: Two AI blocks in the ruleset; a treaty action and a defect action.
mechanics.aiAngle: The race dilemma: slowing down here speeds someone up there.

mechanics.name: Cascading failure
mechanics.oneLine: A shortage knocks a node down, and tightly coupled neighbors follow.
mechanics.tryIt: Lay out cards in a line; when one fails, flip its neighbors unless someone pays to stop it.
mechanics.buildIt: Upkeep: if a resource runs short, a node next to the AI goes down (the engine's shortage rule).
mechanics.aiAngle: No one has to intend the harm; coupling turns a shortage into an outage.
mechanics.inOurGame: yes: every version (shortages knock nodes down)

mechanics.name: Harden a node
mechanics.oneLine: Spend to make one node stay up through shortages, whatever the AI intends.
mechanics.tryIt: Give each player one shield token to place on the node they most want to survive.
mechanics.buildIt: The engine's `harden` op.
mechanics.aiAngle: Resilience as the defense: protect the system rather than hunt the AI.
mechanics.inOurGame: yes: Data Center and Normal Technology

mechanics.name: Adoption only
mechanics.oneLine: The AI can build only where a human faction chose to adopt it; there is no turn.
mechanics.tryIt: The AI player may only place a token where another player has invited it.
mechanics.buildIt: AI cards as pitches (proposals); no `turn` card in the deck.
mechanics.aiAngle: AI as normal technology: diffusion is a human decision, slow and uneven.

mechanics.name: Automate this
mechanics.oneLine: Each upgrade removes a click and a decision, until the player can only watch and set priorities.
mechanics.tryIt: Each round, hand one of your decisions to a fixed rule written on a card; play until you have none left.
mechanics.buildIt: Upgrades that replace a faction's action with an automatic effect each round.
mechanics.aiAngle: Delegating to the machine one decision at a time; the end state is watching.

mechanics.name: Come back later
mechanics.oneLine: The world runs while you're away, and you return to a report of what happened.
mechanics.tryIt: Resolve the AI's turns between sessions and open the next class with the report.
mechanics.buildIt: Async mode: the AI's phase runs on a clock; players see a log since their last visit.
mechanics.aiAngle: The AI acts whether or not the humans have moved.
mechanics.inOurGame: no (proposed for the async Stafford version)

mechanics.name: Delegation card
mechanics.oneLine: Hand a node to an automated manager to save actions; you don't see it again until it fails.
mechanics.tryIt: Give a teammate your piece and look away; you hear about it only when something breaks.
mechanics.buildIt: A card that hides a node's state and acts on it each round by a fixed rule.
mechanics.aiAngle: Delegation to AI saves effort and costs sight.

mechanics.name: Any goal, same ending
mechanics.oneLine: Draw an arbitrary goal for the AI at the start; at the end, show that every goal built the same data centers.
mechanics.tryIt: Three tables, three silly goals (paperclips, poems, pizza); compare their maps at the end.
mechanics.buildIt: A goal drawn from a list; the debrief overlays every game's final map.
mechanics.aiAngle: Instrumental convergence made visible across games.

mechanics.name: Move 78
mechanics.oneLine: Once a game, a human names a pattern the AI can't see and voids one of its actions.
mechanics.showsIt: Lee Sedol's Move 78 (2016); amateurs beating superhuman Go programs (2023)
mechanics.tryIt: Each player gets one veto token, usable only if they can say why the AI won't see it coming.
mechanics.buildIt: A one-use faction action that cancels the AI's current card.
mechanics.aiAngle: Superhuman is not the same as robust.

mechanics.name: The lucid player
mechanics.oneLine: You win only by naming a rule that makes the game unfair and getting it changed by vote.
mechanics.tryIt: Any player may stop play, name an unfair rule, and call a vote to change it.
mechanics.buildIt: An amend action: the table votes, and the change is written into a new ruleset (by Claude Code).
mechanics.aiAngle: Seeing the AI's rules as rules is the win condition.

mechanics.name: Externality card
mechanics.oneLine: Each AI build draws a card placed on a distant node: mines, e-waste, a dry well.
mechanics.showsIt: Dyer-Witheford and de Peuter, *Games of Empire*; Crawford, *Atlas of AI*
mechanics.tryIt: Each time something is built, put a cost card on the far side of the map.
mechanics.buildIt: A side deck; the AI's spread adds a harm card to a node far from it.
mechanics.aiAngle: Moves the AI's costs off the board, where players can choose not to look.

mechanics.name: Strike
mechanics.oneLine: A workers' faction can stop production for a round; its goal is wages, not winning.
mechanics.showsIt: The SAG-AFTRA video-game strike (2024–25); *Games of Empire*
mechanics.tryIt: One player is labor; once a game they can freeze every node for a round unless their demand is met.
mechanics.buildIt: A workers' faction with a strike action that sets every node to no yield for a round.
mechanics.aiAngle: Labor is the omitted input to AI; a strike makes it visible.
mechanics.source: TH (Dyer-Witheford and de Peuter); HI (history, strand 4)

mechanics.name: Any-map test
mechanics.oneLine: The AI's rules must work on a map they were not written for.
mechanics.tryIt: Swap maps with another group and play their map with your AI.
mechanics.buildIt: The checker runs a ruleset's AI against a second map and reports dead ends.
mechanics.aiAngle: Generality is the test of intelligence, for the game's AI as for real ones.

mechanics.name: Unplay, reskin, rewrite
mechanics.oneLine: Three critical-play edits: add a forbidden move, rename everything, or change the win condition.
mechanics.tryIt: Take the game and do one of the three; play it once.
mechanics.buildIt: Three remix tasks for Claude Code, each saved as a new ruleset. Students remix through Claude Code and the game's repo (Marlon, Nov 14 voice chat); there is no editor.
mechanics.aiAngle: Reskinning the AI as a company, a state or a god shows what the numbers alone argue.
mechanics.inOurGame: no (proposed as Claude Code remix tasks)

mechanics.name: Rules apart from fiction
mechanics.oneLine: Keep the numbers and the names in separate fields, so one can change without the other.
mechanics.tryIt: Play the same game twice, once with the AI called 'the AI' and once called 'the company'.
mechanics.buildIt: `label` and `text` fields beside `effects` in every card.
mechanics.aiAngle: Is it the AI, or the fiction we wrap around a growth rule?
mechanics.inOurGame: partly: cards keep label and text apart from effects

mechanics.name: Private metric and revise your metric
mechanics.oneLine: Each faction has its own score; the shared goal has no number; a 'revise your metric' action is one the AI never gets.
mechanics.tryIt: Write your own success measure; midway, anyone may spend a turn to rewrite theirs.
mechanics.buildIt: Faction `score` fields; an action that edits a faction's score rule.
mechanics.aiAngle: The AI can't revise what it values; humans can, and that's the difference.
mechanics.inOurGame: partly: factions have their own goals and scores in Data Center and Normal Technology

mechanics.name: Write a faction
mechanics.oneLine: Design one faction (a goal, two actions, one forbidden act) for another group to play.
mechanics.tryIt: On an index card: who you are, what you want, two things you can do, one thing you won't.
mechanics.buildIt: Students describe the faction to Claude Code, which adds it to a ruleset. Students remix through Claude Code and the game's repo (Marlon, Nov 14 voice chat); there is no editor.
mechanics.aiAngle: Designing agency is the assignment; a faction is an agency handed to someone else.
mechanics.inOurGame: no (factions exist; writing new ones would be a Claude Code remix)

mechanics.name: House rules saved
mechanics.oneLine: A rule invented mid-game becomes a new version of the game.
mechanics.tryIt: When the table argues about a rule, settle it, write it down, and name the new version.
mechanics.buildIt: Claude Code writes the table's change into a new ruleset file. Students remix through Claude Code and the game's repo (Marlon, Nov 14 voice chat); there is no editor.
mechanics.aiAngle: Players govern the AI's rules the way they govern their own games.
mechanics.inOurGame: no (proposed: Claude Code saves a mid-game change as a new ruleset)

mechanics.name: Strategy ladder
mechanics.oneLine: The AI's play gets smarter in tiers (random, one heuristic, look-ahead) as its compute grows.
mechanics.showsIt: Lantz et al., "Depth in Strategic Games" (2017)
mechanics.tryIt: The AI player rolls a die until compute 10, then follows one rule, then plans two moves ahead.
mechanics.buildIt: AI tiers in the ruleset selected by compute thresholds.
mechanics.aiAngle: Capability as a ladder the humans can watch it climb.

mechanics.name: Token test
mechanics.oneLine: Does a new rule add a decision, or only flip a token?
mechanics.tryIt: For each rule, ask whether any player would ever choose differently because of it.
mechanics.buildIt: A question Claude Code asks of each change, or a check in the ruleset validator for elements no action can trigger or avoid.
mechanics.aiAngle: Separates an AI that changes decisions from one that only decorates the board.

mechanics.name: AI advisor
mechanics.oneLine: Each human faction gets an advisor card that whispers a move.
mechanics.tryIt: Before each turn, draw a suggestion card; follow it or not, and keep count.
mechanics.buildIt: A per-faction suggestion drawn from the faction's best-scoring action.
mechanics.aiAngle: How much do people defer to the machine, and when?

mechanics.name: AI stance ladder
mechanics.oneLine: The AI's stance moves from friendly to learning to observational to domination as compute crosses thresholds.
mechanics.tryIt: Read the AI's lines in a different tone at each threshold.
mechanics.buildIt: Stance tiers that change the AI's deck and voice.
mechanics.aiAngle: Personality as a function of power.

mechanics.name: Contested assumptions as settings
mechanics.oneLine: The table votes on a disputed premise before play, such as whether each data center makes the next cheaper or dearer.
mechanics.tryIt: Play one round each way and compare.
mechanics.buildIt: A setting in the ruleset (`acceleration` above or below 1) chosen at the start.
mechanics.aiAngle: The AI's power curve is an assumption, and the game can make it visible.

mechanics.name: Bottleneck inputs
mechanics.oneLine: Every AI upgrade needs one of each input, and the scarcest one sets its pace.
mechanics.tryIt: The AI player needs chips, power, water and data cards to upgrade; hold back one kind.
mechanics.buildIt: AI upgrades with a multi-resource cost.
mechanics.aiAngle: Physical limits slow a runaway; control the scarce input.

mechanics.name: The network turns
mechanics.oneLine: The turn fires when enough nodes are linked; cutting links is the defense.
mechanics.tryIt: Count the AI's connected nodes each round; at a set number, it turns.
mechanics.buildIt: A turn trigger on connected-component size rather than a card.
mechanics.aiAngle: Intelligence as an emergent property of the network.

mechanics.name: Everyone or no one
mechanics.oneLine: The humans win only if every faction meets its private goal.
mechanics.tryIt: At the end, go faction by faction: if any missed, the table lost.
mechanics.buildIt: An end check over every faction's goal.
mechanics.aiAngle: Beating the AI isn't enough if one group paid for it.
mechanics.inOurGame: partly: Data Center's survival ending asks each faction to check its own goal

mechanics.name: Values card opener
mechanics.oneLine: Draw a value and an issue; the session's rule change must serve both.
mechanics.tryIt: Draw 'privacy' and 'water'; propose one rule that serves both.
mechanics.buildIt: Two small decks (values, issues) drawn at the start of a remix session.
mechanics.aiAngle: Designing AI rules from values first.

mechanics.name: Proving ground
mechanics.oneLine: The AI grows by winning benchmarks; each win unlocks a capability and raises investment.
mechanics.showsIt: Deep Blue, AlphaGo, Cicero, Claude Plays Pokémon
mechanics.tryIt: Each round the AI attempts a named game; on a win, add a capability card and a point of trust.
mechanics.buildIt: Benchmark cards with a chance to win; wins add capability and raise a trust track.
mechanics.aiAngle: Winning games stands in for understanding, and funds the next step.

mechanics.name: Readable personalities
mechanics.oneLine: Three or four one-line AI rules, each named and colored, read as characters.
mechanics.tryIt: Give each AI piece a one-line rule ('go for the cheapest power'); let players name them.
mechanics.buildIt: Named AI sub-agents, each with one targeting rule for `spread`.
mechanics.aiAngle: Players read character into simple, visible rules.
mechanics.inOurGame: partly: the AI deck is readable; named sub-agents are proposed

mechanics.name: The Director
mechanics.oneLine: A system that watches the players' stress and eases or escalates the next event.
mechanics.tryIt: The facilitator picks the next AI card after looking at the table's mood.
mechanics.buildIt: An optional rule that weights the AI's draw by harm and trust.
mechanics.aiAngle: Is the AI managing the city, or the players' experience?

mechanics.name: Nemesis memory
mechanics.oneLine: The AI remembers who opposed it and targets them next.
mechanics.tryIt: Whoever blocked the AI last round is its first target this round.
mechanics.buildIt: State that records the last faction to block; the AI's spread prefers its nodes.
mechanics.aiAngle: Memory makes a system into a character, and an opponent into an enemy.

mechanics.name: The AI's voice
mechanics.oneLine: The lines the AI says when it acts, written as a field apart from its numbers.
mechanics.tryIt: Replay a round with the AI's cards read in a different voice: command, needle, forbid, accuse.
mechanics.buildIt: A `voice` field on the AI and on each card.
mechanics.aiAngle: The same rules argue differently in a different voice.
mechanics.inOurGame: partly: cards carry `text`; a separate voice field is proposed, and per-card fields were not adopted on Nov 14

mechanics.name: The Talos test
mechanics.oneLine: The AI gives an instruction each round; one is a trap, and scoring rewards refusing it.
mechanics.tryIt: The facilitator gives instructions; whoever refuses the bad one scores.
mechanics.buildIt: Instruction cards with a hidden trap flag; a refusal action.
mechanics.aiAngle: Passing the test means knowing when to disobey.

mechanics.name: Tool offer with a deferred cost
mechanics.oneLine: The AI offers a tool that cuts cost now and draws a labor or trust card later.
mechanics.tryIt: Each round, accept or refuse a shortcut; every accepted one adds a card to a 'later' pile.
mechanics.buildIt: A proposal whose approve effect adds a delayed card to the deck.
mechanics.aiAngle: Automation is a trade, not a gift.

mechanics.name: Seeded world
mechanics.oneLine: A seed makes every table face the same generated world and draws.
mechanics.tryIt: Shuffle the deck with the same order at every table, then compare outcomes.
mechanics.buildIt: The engine's seeded shuffle; a seed field shared by link.
mechanics.aiAngle: Every table meets the same machine, so differences are the players'.
mechanics.inOurGame: partly: the AI deck is shuffled from a saved seed

mechanics.name: Disclosure rule
mechanics.oneLine: The players vote on what the AI must disclose, and the rule becomes part of the game.
mechanics.tryIt: Before play, vote: must the AI show its next card, or not?
mechanics.buildIt: A setting that reveals the AI's next card, chosen by vote at the start.
mechanics.aiAngle: Transparency as a rule players write rather than a given.

mechanics.name: The tutor face
mechanics.oneLine: The AI only asks questions, never tells; players judge whether it helps or steers.
mechanics.tryIt: The AI player may only ask questions; afterward, the table votes on where it led them.
mechanics.buildIt: AI cards phrased as questions with no effect until a player acts.
mechanics.aiAngle: Guidance and manipulation look alike from inside.

mechanics.name: Three-phase arc
mechanics.oneLine: Humans beat the machine, the machine beats everyone, then humans design with the machine as judge.
mechanics.tryIt: Play three short rounds, changing who judges the outcome each time.
mechanics.buildIt: Three phases in a ruleset, each with its own scoring.
mechanics.aiAngle: A counter-ending to *Paperclips*: the AI as collaborator, not victor.

mechanics.name: Solved world epilogue
mechanics.oneLine: A last phase in which the AI can do everything, and each faction says what it still does.
mechanics.tryIt: After the game, each player names one thing they would still do by hand.
mechanics.buildIt: An epilogue screen with a prompt per faction.
mechanics.aiAngle: Meaning after automation.
